section_summary: This section records diplomatic and business responses to Japan’s 1934 Petroleum Industry Law, especially its import quotas, storage requirements, price controls, and effects on foreign oil companies. It includes British and Netherlands representations, instructions for an American approach to Japan, and a Tokyo despatch with translated Japanese legislative proceedings and an official’s lecture explaining the law.

subfiles.title: Japanese Petroleum Industry Law, concluding articles
subfiles.about: Concluding provisions regulate petroleum refiners and importers, enforcement, penalties, and transition to the new law.
subfiles.summary: The surviving Japanese text covers licensing and supervision of petroleum refining and importing, government powers, penalties, and supplementary provisions for businesses operating when the law takes effect.

subfiles.title: Telegram from London on British response to American oil proposals
subfiles.about: Reports a British official’s initial reaction to American proposals concerning Japan’s petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: The official welcomed the proposals but feared difficulty securing cooperation from smaller American companies; no further Foreign Office response had arrived.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Netherland commercial counselor
subfiles.about: Records Netherlands instructions to seek changes to Japanese petroleum regulations.
subfiles.summary: Kleijn Molekamp told Hamilton and Hornbeck that the Netherland Minister in Tokyo had been instructed to make friendly representations about compulsory storage, annually changeable quotas, and preference for crude oil. The Americans promised to consider the information and keep him informed; a supplement notes that Netherlands interests were thought to exceed American interests.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Teagle asks whether Britain and the Netherlands have protested Japan’s petroleum measures.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck said the Department had received inquiries but no confirmation of protests or proposals for joint action. Teagle undertook to check his information.

subfiles.title: Further telephone conversations with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Teagle presses for an American protest after hearing of British and Netherlands action.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck distinguished the Netherlands’ planned friendly representations from a formal protest, briefed Teagle confidentially, and said the Department awaited word from London.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Netherlands representations in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Netherlands Minister’s approach to Japan’s Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Netherlands aide-mémoire objected to six months’ stocks, annual licensing, harm to refining in the Netherlands Indies, and government price fixing. It sought remedies before Netherlands oil interests committed substantial capital.

subfiles.title: Instructions for American representations to Japan
subfiles.about: Directs an informal oral approach to Japan’s Foreign Minister about the Petroleum Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that compulsory stocks and equipment, government purchase at fixed prices, and uncertain quotas would undermine established American enterprises. It asks Japan to avoid imposing those burdens and requests a telegraphic report after the approach.

subfiles.title: Telegram on earlier British representations
subfiles.about: Explains the British Foreign Office’s earlier approach on Shell’s complaints.
subfiles.summary: A British ambassador had raised Shell’s objections to compulsory tank construction and price fixing in July. The Foreign Office was awaiting a Japanese response or a further request from Shell and suggested a similar American approach.

subfiles.title: Instructions to inform the British Foreign Office of American action
subfiles.about: Directs the embassy to describe American representations and encourage a comparable British approach.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that it had expected British proposals for concurrent action before Japan’s October reporting deadline. It summarizes the American objections to storage, fixed price purchases, and quotas, and asks Britain to convey similar views to Japan.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Tokyo despatch No. 957
subfiles.about: Highlights passages in a Tokyo despatch and its enclosure about foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: The note directs attention to sources of crude, Japanese refining policy, possible retaliation, foreign company quotas, and stock costs.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Petroleum Industry Law and recent effects on foreign oil companies in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew reviews Diet testimony and Kishi Sakai’s lecture, stressing Japan’s goals of stockpiling and expanding domestic refining. He reports evasive official assurances to foreign companies and gasoline quotas that preserve Rising Sun’s volume but reduce Standard-Vacuum’s through an uncorrected clerical error. Standard-Vacuum protested both its quota and the cost and risk of compulsory storage.

subfiles.title: Excerpts from Diet committee hearings on the Petroleum Industry Bill
subfiles.from: Diet committee proceedings; compilation by Rising Sun Petroleum Company and Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Collects officials’ and members’ statements on the aims and operation of Japan’s proposed petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: The excerpts discuss foreign companies, supply sources, import licensing and quotas, price control, and the planned six months’ oil stocks. Officials defend domestic refining and reserves for national defense while repeatedly saying existing imports should not immediately be cut. Further sections address storage costs and locations, subsidies, mergers, small refineries, tankers, ship fuel, and exports.

subfiles.title: Lecture by Kishi Sakai on the Oil Industry Law
subfiles.about: Explains the law’s policy goals, permits, annual business plans, and oil stock requirements.
subfiles.summary: Sakai describes the law as a way to develop domestic refining, regulate imports, and secure petroleum against emergencies. He outlines licensing standards, annual approval of refiners’ and importers’ plans, sales quotas, and detailed rules for storing specified grades of gasoline, crude oil, and heavy oil. The lecture continues beyond this section.
